title: Structural Traits Regulate Canopy Phosphate Processing and Phosphorus Inputs in Native Trees of the Northern Tropical Andes
content:
ABSTRACT

The fragmentation of Andean forests has increased canopy heterogeneity, potentially altering the redistribution of limiting nutrients such as phosphate (PO4–P) through rainfall partitioning. However, the role of canopy traits in modulating phosphate processing and phosphorus inputs remains poorly understood. We evaluated rainfall partitioning and canopy-mediated phosphate dynamics in 20 trees belonging to four native species—Andesanthus lepidotus, Brunellia boqueronensis, Clusia multiflora and Croton magdalenensis—growing in a modified montane forest landscape in the northern Colombian Andes. Over 21 consecutive weeks, throughfall and stemflow were collected weekly, and six structural canopy traits were measured for each tree. On average, throughfall represented 74% of incident precipitation, whereas stemflow contributed less than 1%. Despite its low volume, stemflow was a disproportionately important pathway of phosphorus input, with mean stemflow fluxes reaching 0.180 mg PO4–P m−2 in C. magdalenensis and 0.120 mg PO4–P m−2 in B. boqueronensis, whereas mean throughfall fluxes remained lower across species (0.027–0.059 mg PO4–P m−2). Concentration-based patterns were consistent with strong canopy phosphate processing during rainfall passage, with mean stemflow PO4–P concentrations reaching 2.90 ± 5.74 mg L−1 in C. magdalenensis and 1.09 ± 1.57 mg L−1 in C. multiflora, compared with 0.23 ± 0.11 mg L−1 in bulk rainfall. Structural traits contributed differently to these two dimensions: Canopy density was the clearest predictor of phosphorus fluxes, whereas crown area, leaf area and epiphyte cover were more strongly associated with phosphate enrichment within canopy water. These findings highlight stemflow as a disproportionately important pathway of phosphorus input and show that structural traits regulate both the chemical modification of rainfall and the fine-scale heterogeneity of phosphorus inputs in modified tropical montane forests.
